title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada syndrome constitutes a multisystem autoimmune disorder characterized by granulomatous inflammation targeting melanocyte-containing tissues, including the uveal tract, meninges, inner ear, and skin. The condition is a significant cause of noninfectious uveitis worldwide, although the incidence in the US remains low. Pathogenesis is attributed to T cell–mediated immune responses against melanocytic antigens in genetically susceptible individuals, with increased prevalence among patients of Asian, Hispanic, Middle Eastern, and Native American ancestry.

title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Clinical manifestations typically evolve through prodromal, acute uveitic, and convalescent phases, with bilateral panuveitis, serous retinal detachments, headache, meningismus, tinnitus, dysacusis, vitiligo, poliosis, and alopecia. Diagnosis is clinical and supported by ocular imaging and cerebrospinal fluid analysis when indicated. Management requires prompt initiation of high-dose systemic corticosteroids followed by immunomodulatory therapy to prevent recurrence. Delayed or inadequate treatment elevates the risk of chronic recurrent inflammation, cataract, glaucoma, subretinal fibrosis, and permanent visual impairment. Prognosis depends on early recognition and sustained immunosuppression.

title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome -- Introduction
content: Vogt–Koyanagi–Harada (VKH) syndrome is a multisystem disorder affecting vision and hearing. Historical descriptions date to the 12th century, but the eponym derives from 3 20th-century physicians who characterized the condition's manifestations. Alfred Vogt initially reported bilateral iridocyclitis and eyebrow depigmentation in 1906. Yoshizo Koyanagi later described bilateral serous retinal detachments associated with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) pleocytosis in 1929. Einosuke Harada described acute diffuse choroiditis as a hallmark feature of the disease. [1] VKH manifests due to loss of immune tolerance to melanocytes within the meninges, eyes, skin, hair, and ears. [2]

title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome -- Introduction
content: VKH syndrome exhibits a distinct phenotypic profile across early and late stages. Although clinical findings are identifiable, the underlying pathophysiologic mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Recent technological advancements have clarified several aspects of VKH syndrome, including genetic predisposition and immunologic mechanisms. Ophthalmic complications are frequent, and prompt recognition combined with early therapeutic intervention reduces morbidity and improves long-term visual outcomes. [3] [4]

title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome -- Etiology
content: VKH syndrome is classically considered a spectrum of disorders. Vogt–Koyanagi syndrome represents the anterior presentation, characterized by severe anterior uveitis and extraocular manifestations, including vitiligo, alopecia, poliosis, and dysacusis. Harada disease comprises the severe posterior presentation, including posterior uveitis with diffuse choroiditis and meningeal involvement, often accompanied by CSF abnormalities. The term "Vogt–Koyanagi–Harada syndrome" encompasses the complete disorder, combining both anterior and posterior features. [6]

title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome -- Etiology
content: The precise etiology of VKH syndrome remains incompletely defined. Current evidence suggests the development of T cell–mediated immunity (type IV hypersensitivity) targeting melanocytes following exposure to an inciting viral or environmental factor. [7] Cytomegalovirus and Epstein–Barr virus have been implicated, although no definitive causal relationship has been established. [8] [9] The disease results from loss of immune tolerance to melanocytes, leading to nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation in ocular, auditory, cutaneous, and hair tissues. [10]

title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome -- Etiology
content: VKH syndrome is strongly associated with specific human leukocyte antigen (HLA) class II genes, particularly HLA-DR4, and the allelic variants HLA-DRB10405 and HLA-DRB10410. [11] [12] HLA-DQ4 represents a significant risk factor, especially in Japanese populations, frequently occurring in linkage disequilibrium with HLA-DR4 alleles. [13] A meta-analysis confirmed the association between VKH and HLA-DR4/DRB104, noting variability in the strength of this relationship across ethnic groups. HLA-DRB10404, *0405, and *0410 were identified as risk suballeles, whereas *0401 confers relative protection. [14]

title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome -- Epidemiology
content: Regional differences exist in the prevalence of VKH syndrome among patients presenting with uveitis. VKH syndrome represents a common cause of panuveitis in Asian countries and the Middle East, including India, Japan, Thailand, and Saudi Arabia. [18] [19] The condition is relatively rare in the US, accounting for only 3% to 4% of referrals to tertiary care centers. [20] Approximately 800 new cases are reported annually in Japan. [21] Population-based Japanese data historically indicated an incidence of approximately 6.5 per million per year and a prevalence of 15.5 per million. Estimates from Western populations are lower, with 1.5 to 6 cases per million per year reported in some US series. [22]

title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome -- Epidemiology
content: Hispanic and Native American predominance has been noted in North American cases of VKH syndrome. [23] Countries in South America with substantial native and Hispanic populations, such as Colombia, have not demonstrated a significant increase in VKH syndrome's incidence compared with the US. [24] [25] Although VKH is traditionally associated with populations with higher skin pigmentation, a study in a predominantly White population identified a higher proportion of White non-Hispanic patients, emphasizing the importance of clinical diagnosis rather than reliance on race or ethnicity alone. [26] Twin studies demonstrate the simultaneous onset of VKH in monozygotic twins, and additional twin and sibling analyses support a significant genetic contribution to disease susceptibility. [27] [28] [29]

title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome -- Epidemiology
content: VKH syndrome typically presents in the 3rd or 4th decade of life, with a reported age range from 3 to 78 years. [30] [31] Pediatric cases tend to be aggressive, longstanding, and difficult to treat, with a higher frequency of subretinal fibrosis. [32] Older patients, generally over 65 years of age, exhibit an increased risk of optic disc hyperemia and choroidal detachments. [33] Female patients are affected more frequently than male patients, with reported female-to-male ratios ranging from 3:2 to 2:1.

content: The pathophysiology of VKH syndrome reflects a complex autoimmune attack primarily targeting melanocyte-containing tissues in genetically susceptible individuals. Strong genetic predisposition is indicated by HLA associations, including HLA-DRB1*0405, HLA-DR4, and DR53 alleles. [34]

title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome -- Pathophysiology
content: Autoreactive CD4+ T-helper type 1 (Th1) and T-helper type 17 (Th17) cells recognize antigens derived from melanocyte-related proteins, such as tyrosinase, tyrosinase-related protein 1, and glycoprotein 100, in pigmented tissues. [35] [36] Immune activation may be triggered or amplified by viral or environmental stimuli, resulting in loss of immune tolerance. [37] Many patients report a prodromal flu-like illness preceding the onset of ocular, auditory, and cutaneous inflammation.

title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome -- Pathophysiology
content: Th1-mediated inflammation specifically targets melanocytes, with the tyrosinase peptide recognized by T cells, particularly in melanocytes expressing HLA-DRB1*0405. [38] Homology between the tyrosinase peptide and cytomegalovirus peptides has been demonstrated. Additional studies have detected Epstein–Barr virus DNA in CSF of patients with VKH using polymerase chain reaction techniques. [39]

title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome -- Pathophysiology
content: The immune response induces granulomatous inflammation of the choroidal stroma (primary stromal choroiditis), characterized by diffuse infiltration of choroidal melanocytes and disruption of the blood–ocular barrier. Choroidal thickening and inflammation lead to multiple serous retinal detachments.

title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome -- Pathophysiology
content: Melanocyte-rich tissues in the meninges, inner ear, skin (vitiligo, poliosis), and hair are also targeted, accounting for the multisystem manifestations of VKH syndrome. Persistent ocular inflammation, which may be subclinical, can progress to chronic depigmentation of the fundus (“sunset-glow fundus”) and structural damage to the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and choriocapillaris. [40]

title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome -- Histopathology
content: Histopathological findings in VKH syndrome include nonnecrotizing, diffuse granulomatous inflammation, in contrast to the focal granulomatous inflammation observed in tuberculosis or sarcoidosis. The choroidal stroma of the uveal tract is primarily affected, with the choriocapillaris largely spared in the acute stage. [41] The infiltrate comprises lymphocytes, epithelioid histiocytes, and multinucleated giant cells, forming granulomas that produce Dalen–Fuchs nodules between the RPE and the Bruch membrane. Hematoxylin and eosin staining of enucleated specimens demonstrates B and T cells within the choroid and loss of choroidal melanocytes. [42]

title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome -- Histopathology
content: Differentiation of VKH syndrome from sympathetic ophthalmia is challenging histologically. Both conditions exhibit sparing of the choriocapillaris in the acute stage, nonnecrotizing diffuse granulomatous uveal inflammation in the acute phase, Dalen–Fuchs nodules, chronic-phase melanocyte loss, and chorioretinal adhesion with scarring and choriocapillaris involvement in the chronic recurrent stage. [43] The history of penetrating ocular injury remains a distinguishing feature unique to sympathetic ophthalmia. [44]

title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome -- Histopathology
content: Recurrent episodes of VKH syndrome produce sunset-glow fundus, characterized by progressive fundus depigmentation in the setting of optic disc pallor, a marker of poor visual prognosis. Late-stage VKH syndrome demonstrates peripheral fundus scars histopathologically composed of chorioretinal atrophy and RPE loss, rather than Dalen–Fuchs nodules as previously thought. [45] [46] [47] Dalen–Fuchs nodules are typically confined to the posterior pole and equator and are observed during the acute phase.

title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome -- Histopathology
content: Histopathologic features vary across disease stages. In the acute stage, diffuse lymphocytic infiltration, primarily T cells with a T-helper/T-suppressor imbalance, and macrophage infiltration affect the uvea, including choroid, ciliary body, and iris. Focal aggregates of epithelioid cells and multinucleated giant cells containing pigment are present, without choroidal necrosis, and serous retinal detachments are common. During the convalescent stage, gradual loss of melanin granules from choroidal melanocytes produces a pale, depigmented fundus, and inflammation is predominantly nongranulomatous. Chronic recurrent disease demonstrates chorioretinal atrophy, scarring, focal hyperpigmentation, choriocapillaris involvement, and granulomatous inflammation.

title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome -- History and Physical
content: Patients with VKH typically present with a combination of systemic, neurological, and ocular manifestations that evolve through distinct clinical stages. The disease primarily affects young to middle-aged individuals, most frequently in the 3rd to 5th decade of life, with a female predominance and higher incidence among Asian, Middle Eastern, Hispanic, and Native American populations. Detailed history taking and recognition of sequential clinical phases are essential for early diagnosis and effective management.

title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome -- History and Physical
content: The prodromal phase often precedes ocular involvement by several days and resembles a viral illness, with headache, fever, malaise, nausea, neck stiffness, and photophobia. These symptoms reflect aseptic meningitis, an immune-mediated inflammation of melanocyte-containing meninges. [49] Cochlear involvement is suggested by tinnitus, vertigo, or hearing loss. [50] Absence of prior ocular trauma or surgery provides an important diagnostic clue, distinguishing VKH syndrome from sympathetic ophthalmia.

title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome -- History and Physical
content: Following the systemic prodrome, the ocular phase typically begins abruptly, presenting with bilateral blurred vision, photophobia, and ocular discomfort. Although both eyes are usually involved, symptoms may initially manifest asymmetrically. Central vision distortion or metamorphopsia may occur due to subretinal fluid accumulation from choroidal inflammation. [51]

title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome -- History and Physical
content: VKH progresses through 4 clinical phases: prodromal, acute uveitic, chronic uveitic (convalescent), and recurrent chronic. The prodromal phase is often self-limited, lasting hours to weeks, and exhibits subtle chorioretinal findings that may be overlooked without indocyanine green angiography (ICGA) and correlation with CSF analysis. [52] [53] Systemic and neurological symptoms may mimic viral meningitis, including headache, neck stiffness, fever, auditory disturbances, dizziness, eye pain, and photophobia. History frequently reveals a recent recovery from a viral illness. Examination may demonstrate mild meningeal signs, and CSF analysis typically shows lymphocytic pleocytosis, confirming central nervous system involvement.

Anterior segment findings include cells and flare in the anterior chamber, mutton-fat keratic precipitates, posterior synechiae, and vitritis. Slit-lamp examination typically reveals vitreous cells.

title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome -- History and Physical
content: Posterior segment involvement demonstrates multiple serous (exudative) retinal detachments, optic disc hyperemia, and choroidal thickening. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) and fundus fluorescein angiography (FFA) reveal pinpoint leakage and pooling of dye. Focal subretinal fluid can coalesce or increase in height without prompt treatment (see Image. Subretinal Fluid in Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome). The optic disc is frequently swollen and hyperemic, occasionally accompanied by hemorrhages or a macular fan or star simulating neuroretinitis (see Image. Optic Disc Edema in Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome).

Posterior segment involvement demonstrates multiple serous (exudative) retinal detachments, optic disc hyperemia, and choroidal thickening. Focal subretinal fluid can coalesce or increase in height without prompt treatment (see Image. Subretinal Fluid in Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome). The optic disc is frequently swollen and hyperemic, occasionally accompanied by hemorrhages or a macular fan or star simulating neuroretinitis (see Image. Optic Disc Edema in Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome).

title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome -- History and Physical
content: Edema secondary to inflammation can extend to the retina, optic nerve, or ciliary body, producing exudative retinal detachment, optic disc edema, and acute angle-closure glaucoma, respectively. title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome -- History and Physical
content: Inferior bullous exudative retinal detachments typically exhibit shifting fluid with changes in body position from sitting to supine (see Image . Inferior Exudative Retinal Detachment in Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome). Chorioretinal folds, including radial or circumferential folds surrounding the optic disc (Paton lines), may be observed. Small, round nodules beneath the RPE (Dalen–Fuchs nodules) are more clearly visualized using multicolor imaging at and around the posterior pole. [55] A 2025 study of 11 patients with serous retinal detachments demonstrated persistent color vision deficits following resolution of subretinal fluid. [56]

content: The chronic or convalescent phase develops following control of acute inflammation. Recovery is characterized by depigmentation of the uveal tract. title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome -- History and Physical
content: Multifocal, small, scalloped atrophic chorioretinal scars, resembling presumed ocular histoplasmosis syndrome (POHS), may appear, particularly in the inferior fundus, often in linear distributions. Histopathologic studies confirm that these lesions represent atrophy rather than Dalen–Fuchs nodules. The hallmark ocular feature of this phase is the sunset-glow fundus, a red depigmented appearance resulting from diffuse choroidal and RPE depigmentation. The Sugiura sign, a perilimbal vitiligo ring, is characteristic.

title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome -- History and Physical
content: The recurrent chronic phase is characterized by recurrent granulomatous anterior uveitis or chronic low-grade inflammation. This phase is frequently associated with complications, including cataract, glaucoma, choroidal neovascularization, iris neovascularization, optic disc neovascularization, and subretinal fibrosis. content: A typical VKH presentation begins with a preceding systemic illness, followed by bilateral visual disturbance and progressive depigmentation of ocular and cutaneous tissues. The disorder represents autoimmune-mediated destruction of melanocytes affecting ocular, meningeal, auditory, and integumentary systems.

title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome -- Evaluation
content: VKH syndrome is a clinical diagnosis based on a characteristic constellation of findings, supported by laboratory and imaging studies. A comprehensive history should assess prior episodes, meningeal symptoms, ocular or orbital pain, and auditory complaints. Physical examination and slit-lamp evaluation may demonstrate signs of previous inflammatory episodes. Poliosis or vitiligo typically indicates progression to the chronic uveitic phase of disease.

title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome -- Evaluation -- Ocular Investigations
content: OCT is a noninvasive imaging modality used to evaluate VKH and assist in diagnosis (see Image . Optical Coherence Tomography Findings in Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome). ICGA may provide superior sensitivity for monitoring chronic disease and its progression. In acute VKH, OCT can demonstrate intraretinal septated fluid (bacillary layer detachment), subretinal fluid, RPE undulations or corrugations, and increased choroidal volume with diffuse thickening, indicative of choroidal inflammation. [60] OCT constitutes a key component of multimodal imaging to establish VKH diagnosis. [61] [62]

title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome -- Evaluation -- Ocular Investigations
content: Enhanced depth imaging (EDI) or swept-source OCT enables reliable quantification of choroidal thickness and volume, which increase in the acute phase and gradually normalize with systemic corticosteroid and immunosuppressive therapy. In chronic VKH, OCT frequently reveals choroidal thinning, RPE irregularity, outer retinal disruption, and subretinal fibrosis, all associated with poorer visual outcomes and persistent inflammation. Recurrent VKH may present as renewed choroidal thickening or increased choroidal volume on EDI-OCT despite a quiet slit-lamp examination, highlighting OCT’s role as an objective biomarker of subclinical activity. [63]

title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome -- Evaluation -- Ocular Investigations
content: OCT angiography (OCTA) is a dyeless, noninvasive imaging modality under active investigation for VKH diagnosis and follow-up. In acute VKH, OCTA commonly demonstrates discrete flow voids in the choriocapillaris slab, representing areas of reduced perfusion that correspond to hypofluorescent lesions on ICGA and hyporeflective spots on EDI-OCT. Studies indicate that both the number and area of these flow voids decrease following initiation of high-dose systemic corticosteroids and immunosuppressive therapy, paralleling clinical improvement and ICGA normalization. [64]

title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome -- Evaluation -- Ocular Investigations
content: Widefield swept-source OCTA reveals reduced superficial and deep retinal capillary density in acute VKH, with partial recovery over time, suggesting microvascular alterations may extend beyond the choriocapillaris and potentially affect retinal function. Despite these advantages, OCTA remains complementary to ICGA due to limitations in the field of view, motion sensitivity, segmentation artifacts, and the lack of standardized quantitative metrics. [65]

title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome -- Evaluation -- Ocular Investigations
content: Fundus autofluorescence (FAF) imaging demonstrates variable patterns in VKH disease, aiding noninvasive assessment of RPE changes across disease stages. In acute VKH with serous retinal detachment, short-wavelength (SW-AF) and near-infrared (NIR-AF) FAF show hypoautofluorescent signals due to blockage by subretinal fluid. A background of mild, uniform hyperautofluorescence appears in patients imaged soon after symptom onset, while diffuse, mottled hyperautofluorescence develops in patients imaged weeks later. [66] Postresolution, numerous hypoautofluorescent granular dots appear in previously detached areas, indicating RPE damage or atrophy and correlating with FFA window defects. [67]

content: Chronic VKH exhibits both hypoautofluorescence and hyperautofluorescence. Hypoautofluorescence links to peripapillary atrophy, scars, or RPE loss, while hyperautofluorescence associates with cystoid macular edema or RPE proliferation. Sunset-glow fundus, from choroidal depigmentation, shows no significant FAF change, distinguishing this finding from true RPE atrophy. [68] Ultra-widefield FAF highlights peripheral abnormalities in chronic cases, including multifocal hypoautofluorescent spots, hyperautofluorescent spots, and lattice-like patterns. [69]

title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome -- Evaluation -- Ocular Investigations
content: B-scan ultrasonography remains valuable in VKH, particularly when media opacities, such as dense vitritis or cataract, limit fundus visualization. [70] In acute VKH, B-scan typically shows diffuse, low- to medium-reflective choroidal thickening, with posterior predominance and bilateral involvement, indicating intense choroidal stromal inflammation (see Image . B-Scan Ultrasonography Findings in Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome). [71] Smooth, dome-shaped serous retinal detachments with acoustically clear subretinal fluid are frequently observed and correlate with sudden visual decline. Serial scans during treatment demonstrate gradual normalization of choroidal thickness and retinal reattachment, providing objective confirmation of therapeutic response. [72]

content: Ultrasound biomicroscopy (UBM) in VKH shows a thickened, swollen ciliary body with low internal reflectivity and obscured ciliary processes, reflecting intense uveal inflammation. title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome -- Evaluation -- Ocular Investigations
content: FFA in acute VKH typically demonstrates multiple pinpoint hyperfluorescent leaks, with fluorescence that increases in size and intensity over time, producing a “starry sky” pattern (see Image . Pinpoint Leakage on Fluorescein Angiography). Leaks occur at the level of the RPE in the early phase, with pooling of dye in subretinal spaces during the late phase (see Image . Late-Phase Fluorescein Angiography in Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome). Early-phase FFA may also show focal or patchy areas of choroidal hypofluorescence, indicating delayed choroidal filling (see Image . Early-Phase Fluorescein Angiography in Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome). [75] Optic disc leakage and serous detachment of the neurosensory retina are frequently observed. Placoid subretinal areas of dye pooling may occur in some patients in the late phase. Retinal paravascular staining suggestive of retinal vasculitis may be noted. Alternate bands of hyperfluorescence and hypofluorescence indicate choroidal folds.

title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome -- Evaluation -- Ocular Investigations
content: ICGA may be used for diagnostic purposes and is highly valuable for monitoring disease activity and treatment response. [77] ICGA directly evaluates the choroid and RPE, the 2 structures most affected in the early course of VKH. The wavelengths used in ICGA penetrate the choroid effectively with reduced interference from the RPE compared to FFA. [78] Studies report 90% to 100% sensitivity for ICGA in diagnosing VKH. [79] ICGA is considered the gold standard for detecting choroidal stromal inflammation.

title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome -- Evaluation -- Ocular Investigations
content: Acute-stage ICGA typically demonstrates multiple hypofluorescent dark dots representing choroidal granulomas, along with diffuse choroidal hyperfluorescence that often persists longer than FFA abnormalities. [80] Key ICGA findings include early choroidal stromal vessel hyperfluorescence and leakage; hypofluorescent dark dots; fuzzy vascular pattern of large stromal vessels in the intermediate phase; and disc hyperfluorescence. Hypofluorescent dark dots are the most consistent and prominent sign, resolving 90% to 100% after 4 months of therapy. Other findings, including early stromal vessel hyperfluorescence, fuzzy intermediate-phase vessels, and disc hyperfluorescence, resolve within 2 months of treatment.

content: Treatment consisted of pulse intravenous methylprednisolone (IVMP) 500 to 1,000 mg for 3 days, followed by high-dose oral corticosteroids (0.8–1.5 mg/kg) tapered slowly. Immunosuppressive agents were added for insufficient response. ICGA is particularly useful for detecting subclinical choroidal activity during immunosuppression tapering, as hypofluorescent dark spots may appear even when clinical signs and FFA findings are unremarkable. [81]

content: Multifocal and full-field electroretinography may demonstrate reduced amplitudes, indicating diffuse photoreceptor dysfunction in eyes with recurrent or chronic VKH, even when best-corrected visual acuity remains relatively preserved. Visual field testing frequently demonstrates central or paracentral scotomas and enlarged blind spots during the acute stage, which can progress to more complex defects in chronic disease, reflecting structural macular and optic nerve changes.

title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome -- Evaluation -- Systemic Workup
content: Routine laboratory investigations, including complete blood count, liver and renal function tests, and inflammatory markers such as erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein, are generally nonspecific in VKH. These tests are valuable for excluding infectious etiologies and monitoring treatment safety during systemic corticosteroid or immunosuppressant administration. Targeted serologic tests for syphilis, tuberculosis, sarcoidosis, and other infectious or inflammatory mimickers are essential before confirming VKH, given the overlapping phenotype with other causes of granulomatous uveitis. [82]

title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome -- Evaluation -- Systemic Workup
content: Although no pathognomonic serum biomarker exists, elevated serum immunoglobulin E (IgE) has been associated with more severe vascular leakage, greater macular edema, and poorer visual outcomes in acute VKH, suggesting a potential role as a marker of inflammatory burden. Additional studies have explored correlations between serum immunoglobulin profiles and choroidal or retinal imaging findings, but such markers remain investigational and are not yet incorporated into routine clinical decision-making. [83]

title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome -- Evaluation -- Systemic Workup
content: CSF analysis in the prodromal or early acute phase frequently shows lymphocytic pleocytosis with elevated protein and normal glucose, consistent with aseptic meningitis and reflecting inflammation of melanocyte-rich meninges. CSF abnormalities appear in a high proportion of early VKH cases and typically resolve with systemic corticosteroid therapy. Lumbar puncture is most informative when performed near symptom onset in patients with neurological manifestations, such as headache or neck stiffness.

[84] MRI also helps exclude infectious meningitis, demyelinating disease, or neoplastic processes, increasing diagnostic confidence when combined with ocular and CSF findings.

content: Audiological evaluation often reveals bilateral, predominantly high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL), even when patients report only subtle tinnitus or aural fullness. [85] These findings reflect autoimmune inflammation targeting the cochlea and vestibular apparatus and may fluctuate with systemic disease activity and immunosuppressive therapy.

title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome -- Evaluation -- Systemic Workup
content: VKH demonstrates a strong genetic association with HLA-DR4 alleles, particularly HLA-DRB1*0405, across multiple ethnic populations, supporting a major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class II–restricted autoimmune response against melanocyte antigens. These alleles likely facilitate presentation of melanocyte-derived peptides, such as tyrosinase, to autoreactive T cells, lowering the disease threshold in susceptible individuals. [87] Immunologic profiling reveals a predominant Th1 and Th17 signature, with elevated interferon-γ and IL-17 levels in blood and intraocular fluid during active disease. [88] IL-17F (rs763780) polymorphisms correlate with increased susceptibility in Chinese Han patients, indicating a contributory role of IL-17–mediated immunity in pathogenesis. [89]

title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome -- Treatment / Management
content: Acute VKH was historically managed primarily with high-dose systemic corticosteroids, typically beginning with IVMP 1,000 mg daily for 3 consecutive days, followed by oral prednisolone 1 to 2 mg/kg/day with gradual tapering over a minimum of 6 months. [90] [91] [92] Extended systemic corticosteroid therapy (≥6 months) has been associated with lower relapse rates and improved visual outcomes compared with shorter courses. A study demonstrated that early withdrawal of oral corticosteroids increased the risk of recurrence more than 8 times. [93]

title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome -- Treatment / Management
content: Posterior sub-Tenon (PST) injection of triamcinolone may be considered in addition to systemic therapy, particularly in patients who cannot tolerate systemic therapy or have contraindications. [95] Use of local therapy alone in a systemic disease such as VKH remains controversial and is not routinely practiced. [96] Risks of elevated IOP and cataract formation, as well as alternative therapeutic options, require discussion prior to periocular or intraocular steroid administration. [97]

title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome -- Treatment / Management
content: Conventional IMT agents, including MTX, mycophenolate mofetil (MMF), azathioprine, CsA, and tacrolimus, control inflammation in 60% to 90% of patients when combined with tapering steroids. MTX (7.5–25 mg/week) induces remission in approximately 50% of cases but may have high relapse rates, up to 50%, and requires 3 to 6 months for peak effect. MMF (1–3 g/day), the most commonly used 1st-line IMT agent, controlled acute VKH in 50% of cases in a series but required augmentation in 1/2 of those cases. CsA (2–5 mg/kg/day) is effective in chronic VKH but carries a high discontinuation rate, sometimes exceeding 60%, due to renal toxicity and hypertension. [105]

title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Sympathetic ophthalmia presents with bilateral serous retinal detachments, papillitis, multifocal pinpoint leaks on FFA, and hypofluorescent dark spots on ICGA, which may be clinically indistinguishable from VKH if a history of penetrating ocular trauma is unknown. [112] Sympathetic ophthalmia is typically distinguished by a history of ocular penetrating trauma or surgery, which is a hallmark feature and is excluded by VKH diagnostic criteria. The uveitis pattern in sympathetic ophthalmia is often unpredictable, unlike VKH’s staged progression, and systemic features are uncommon. [113] [114]

title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Central serous chorioretinopathy (CSCR) can present with serous retinal detachments, particularly following systemic corticosteroid use. Features of intraocular inflammation are absent in CSCR, and the condition is usually asymmetric. OCT demonstrates serous pigment epithelial detachments with a straight RPE, in contrast to the RPE undulations observed in VKH. [115] FFA in CSCR shows characteristic inkblot, smoke-stack, or diffuse leaks without optic disc hyperfluorescence, whereas VKH exhibits multiple pinpoint leaks with a hot optic disc. [116] CSCR typically resolves after cessation of steroids, while VKH requires systemic corticosteroid therapy for management.

content: Acute APMPPE and VKH share several clinical features. Both conditions can present with a preceding viral or flu-like prodrome, headache, and rapid visual loss, accompanied by yellowish-white placoid lesions in the fundus. [117] [118] Some authors have proposed that APMPPE and VKH may represent a spectrum of related disease processes. [119] [120]

title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome -- Prognosis
content: VKH may have a relatively favorable prognosis if treated early and effectively. Prognosis worsens cumulatively with recurrent disease episodes. Poor prognostic indicators include age at disease onset and the frequency of recurrences. Sunset-glow fundus, a marker of the most severe stage of VKH and an indicator of poor visual function, can develop even when earlier-stage clinical findings are controlled. [129] Comparative studies demonstrate that combination therapy with corticosteroids and supplementary IMT significantly reduces sunset-glow fundus rates from 60% to 16%. Rates of subretinal fibrosis, an untreatable complication that can cause permanent vision loss, also decrease from 34% to 16% in patients treated early with combination therapy. [130]

title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome -- Prognosis
content: A study of 68 patients with acute VKH evaluated prognostic factors for visual outcomes, complications, and recurrent inflammation. Good initial visual acuity (better than 20/200), prolonged corticosteroid therapy (>9 months) with slow tapering, absence of posterior synechiae, and lack of complications or extraocular manifestations predicted final vision of 20/20. Older age, poor initial vision, and posterior synechiae increased complication risk. Rapid corticosteroid tapering, severe anterior chamber inflammation, poor initial vision, and extraocular manifestations were associated with recurrent inflammation. title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome -- Prognosis
content: A separate study of 69 pediatric patients (age < 18 years) found that chronic recurrent VKH correlated with earlier onset, severe anterior chamber reaction, and corneal involvement. Complications included cataract (23.9%), glaucoma (39.1%), and choroidal neovascular membranes (26.1%), with higher rates in recurrent cases. Visual acuity improved from 20/70 to 20/50 overall. Despite complications, most pediatric patients achieved favorable long-term visual outcomes, although recurrent VKH was associated with worse results. [132]

title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome -- Complications
content: VKH is a systemic disease, and complications may include hearing loss, dysacusis, tinnitus, aural fullness, vertigo, vitiligo, and ophthalmic manifestations. [133] SNHL occurs in up to 68% of patients. Most cases of SNHL in VKH resolve with appropriate corticosteroid therapy. [134] [135] IMT has demonstrated efficacy in controlling auditory symptoms. However, some reports indicate limited benefit in patients unable to tolerate corticosteroids. [136] [137] Hearing loss may improve with IMT, although cochlear implants remain necessary in some cases. [138] [139] Intratympanic corticosteroid injection has shown benefit in patients who cannot tolerate systemic corticosteroids. [140] Vertigo is less common, affecting 17% to 19% of patients, but it can cause substantial morbidity. This symptom responds favorably to corticosteroid therapy. [141]

title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome -- Complications
content: VKH can induce ciliary body inflammation and edema during the acute uveitic phase, resulting in anterior rotation of the ciliary body and closure of the anterior segment angle. This process may lead to secondary acute angle-closure glaucoma, a mechanism similar to that observed after topiramate use or panretinal photocoagulation. [144]

title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome -- Complications
content: Patients may develop IOP elevation, with a median value of 32.9 mm Hg (range 27–40 mm Hg). Conventional IOP-lowering therapy is frequently ineffective. The mean age of affected patients is approximately 55.6 years, with a female predominance. Headache accompanied by sudden visual decline is a typical presenting feature. UBM is critical for diagnosing uveal effusion, ciliary body detachment, and anterior rotation of the ciliary body. Management of inflammation with corticosteroids remains the primary strategy for controlling IOP in these cases. [145]

title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome -- Complications
content: Visually significant ophthalmic complications of chronic VKH include cataracts, glaucoma, neovascular glaucoma, macular holes, chronic retinal detachments, subretinal fibrosis, and choroidal neovascularization. title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome -- Complications
content: Cataract surgery generally yields favorable outcomes once inflammation has been controlled for 3 months, with significant visual improvement observed in 99% of eyes. [149] [150] [151] A study reported satisfactory postoperative results with only 1 month of inflammation control using a combination of IMT and corticosteroids. Postoperative complications are uncommon. Approximately 10% of eyes develop hyphema, and 13% experience ocular hypertension, with both conditions typically resolving spontaneously. Consistent with an intraocular inflammatory disorder, posterior capsular opacification develops in up to 50% of patients following phacoemulsification. [152]

title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome -- Complications
content: Ocular hypertension and glaucomatous optic neuropathy are common complications in patients with VKH. Glaucoma develops in approximately 6% to 45% of cases. [153] Significant risk factors for ocular hypertension include uveal effusion, poor visual acuity at initial presentation, delayed treatment initiation, posterior synechiae, and having more than 3 recurrent disease episodes. [154] Long-term topical and systemic corticosteroid therapy also contributes substantially to glaucoma risk in VKH. [155] The primary mechanism of glaucoma in VKH is open-angle rather than steroid-induced. However, a significant proportion of VKH patients develop glaucomatous optic neuropathy secondary to pupillary block caused by posterior synechiae. [156]

title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome -- Complications
content: Subretinal fibrosis represents a significant complication of VKH, often resulting in severe visual decline. Risk factors include pediatric onset, particularly in aggressive or long-standing disease; prolonged symptom duration before treatment; extensive subretinal fluid accumulation, indicative of serous or bullous detachment, at diagnosis; frequent recurrences; and marked ocular inflammation. Subretinal fibrosis develops in up to 40% of eyes with VKH. [157]

content: The onset of subretinal fibrosis occurs earlier in Hispanic patients, approximately 6.5 months after disease onset, compared with 6.5 years in non-Hispanic patients. title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome -- Complications
content: Subretinal fibrosis can precipitate macular detachments, severely compromising vision. Surgical management of these detachments may involve pars plana vitrectomy, excision of subretinal fibrosis, and vitreous tamponade. [159] Additional ocular complications reported in VKH include scleromalacia and choroidal osteoma. Choroidal neovascular membranes develop in 14% to 17% of patients with VKH. These lesions respond to vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) blockade therapy. [160] [161]

title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome -- Complications
content: Pediatric VKH remains a challenging disorder to manage, with a high risk of poor final visual acuity. Chronic recurrent cases present at an earlier age and demonstrate more severe anterior chamber inflammation, with pronounced corneal involvement, including band keratopathy. Complications in this population include corneal involvement, cataract in approximately 24% of cases, glaucoma in approximately 40%, and choroidal neovascular membranes in approximately 26% of cases. [162]

title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome -- Consultations
content: Appropriate referrals are essential for the management of integumentary and auditory manifestations in VKH. Timely consultation with audiology, otorhinolaryngology, and dermatology facilitates ongoing monitoring of disease progression.

title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Patient education is critical to emphasize that VKH is a systemic disease with potential for relapse and recurrence. Untreated recurrent episodes result in progressively worse outcomes, often necessitating lifelong IMT. [163] Patients should be informed about the range of disease manifestations to enable early recognition of relapse. Ongoing management should involve coordinated care from multiple specialists, including neurologists, ophthalmologists, dermatologists, and otorhinolaryngologists.

title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome -- Pearls and Other Issues
content: Although rare, VKH should be considered in patients presenting with eye pain, associated headache, or meningeal signs. Therapeutic goals include controlling clinically apparent disease and preventing progression of VKH complications through early identification and treatment. Corticosteroids remain a cornerstone of therapy, but monotherapy without adjunctive IMT is associated with higher rates of recurrence and complications.

title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: When detected early, VKH syndrome may be effectively managed through coordinated care involving primary care physicians, emergency medicine practitioners, and specialists in low vision, otorhinolaryngology, ophthalmology, neurology, and audiology. [164] Disease manifestations may be subtle, including symptoms that mimic aseptic meningitis, tinnitus, and vague visual disturbances, often accompanied by photophobia, floaters, or blurred vision. [165] Early intervention prevents significant morbidity, particularly from retinal complications. Most vision loss results from repeated cycles of acute inflammation and may occur in the absence of apparent symptoms. Patients are at risk of developing secondary complications without timely management, including severe vision impairment or blindness. [166]
